name: Capitoline Temple of Jupiter
description: Rome's chief civic temple joined Jupiter Optimus Maximus with Juno and Minerva and anchored vows, triumphs, and the public cult.
date_note: The Republican temple and Augustan restorations belong to the AD 1 landscape.

name: Sanctuary of Fortuna Primigenia
description: The terraced sanctuary and its lot oracle made Praeneste one of central Italy's strongest supra-local cult centres.
date_note: The monumental sanctuary predates AD 1; no later imperial rebuilding is implied.

name: Oracle of Apollo at Delphi
description: The Pythian sanctuary remained a Panhellenic place of consultation, dedication, and festival assembly.
date_note: Salona is the closest valid engine anchor and does not relocate Delphi historically.

name: Altis of Olympia
description: Zeus's sacred precinct gathered temples, treasuries, athletic rites, and interstate dedications around the Olympic festival.
date_note: Pontikokastro is the closest valid engine anchor to ancient Olympia.

name: Artemision of Ephesos
description: The great temple of Artemis served Ephesos and attracted worshippers, gifts, and asylum claims from across the eastern Mediterranean.
date_note: Ayasuluk is the valid engine location for Ephesos; the site is not represented as a Christian shrine.

name: Second Temple of Jerusalem
description: The Herodian Temple was the unique sacrificial centre of Judaean religion and the focus of pilgrimage at the campaign opening.
date_note: Valid from AD 1 until the Temple's destruction in AD 70; later rabbinic institutions are not backdated.

name: Nisa Royal Precinct
description: The Arsacid ceremonial complex held dynastic architecture, storerooms, and a powerful ancestral memory close to the Parthian homeland.
date_note: Treated as an Arsacid ancestral-cult anchor rather than evidence for uniform later Zoroastrian orthodoxy.

name: Vajrasana at Bodh Gaya
description: The place of the Buddha's awakening was already marked by Mauryan patronage and drew Buddhist devotion beyond a single school.
date_note: The AD 1 form excludes the surviving later temple superstructure.

name: Stupas of Sanchi
description: Stupas and monastic foundations near Vidisha preserved relic devotion and a major patronage network in central India.
date_note: Bhilsa is the valid engine anchor for Sanchi and Vidisha; sectarian ownership is intentionally shared.

name: Anuradhapura Monastic Precincts
description: Early monasteries around the royal capital joined relic worship, teaching, alms, and court patronage.
date_note: Only foundations established by the first century BCE are represented; later monumental phases are excluded.

name: Kashi Sacred Crossing
description: Kashi's riverfront ritual landscape links sacrifice, purification, learning, and movement along the middle Ganga.
date_note: Importance is restrained because much fuller Puranic pilgrimage evidence is later than AD 1.

name: Kankali Tila Jain Precinct
description: The Mathura complex preserves early Jain stupa, image, donor, and monastic activity at a major north Indian crossroads.
date_note: The site is valid at the era boundary; later Kushan sculpture is not projected backward.

name: Qufu Ancestral Precinct
description: The home landscape of Kongzi supported lineage commemoration and the Han state's growing ritual recognition of the sage.
date_note: The row represents Han commemoration and not the much later architectural complex now visible.

name: Chang'an State Altars
description: Imperial sacrifices around the Han capital ordered Heaven, Earth, ancestors, and the polity through court ritual.
date_note: Represents the Western Han ritual capital at AD 1 without importing later Daoist institutions.

name: Izumo Yayoi Ritual Landscape
description: Communal offerings and bronze-deposit traditions make Izumo a strong regional focus for local deities and ancestors.
date_note: No later Izumo Taisha building or codified Shinto system is backdated.

name: Saro Ancestral Precinct
description: The Gyeongju basin's emerging communities expressed authority through lineage rites, mortuary display, and local sacred landscapes.
date_note: This is an archaeological regional adapter and does not assume later Silla royal ritual.

name: Khangai Sacred Heights
description: Mountain, sky, pasture, and ancestral rites converge in the Khangai heartland of Inner Asian pastoral communities.
date_note: The landscape is ancient; no medieval imperial cult or later written liturgy is implied.

name: Kailash Highland Axis
description: The conspicuous peak and surrounding headwaters form a durable sacred landscape for western Tibetan highland communities.
date_note: The site models local pre-imperial traditions and does not backdate later organized Bon doctrine or pilgrimage circuits.

name: Temple of Amun at Karnak
description: The vast Theban precinct remained a living centre of Amun's cult, priestly estates, procession, and regional memory under Roman rule.
date_note: Only structures and cults extant by AD 1 are intended.

name: Temple of Isis at Philae
description: Isis's island sanctuary linked the First Cataract, Nile travel, Egyptian temple ritual, and worshippers from beyond Egypt.
date_note: Aswan is the nearest valid engine anchor to Philae.

name: Oracle of Amun at Siwa
description: The oasis oracle joined Libyan, Egyptian, and Greek religious worlds and retained prestige long after Alexander's consultation.
date_note: Shared access represents an ancient frontier cult and not religious homogenization.

name: Jebel Barkal and the Temple of Amun
description: The sacred sandstone mountain and its temples bound Napatan kingship, Amun worship, and the memory of Kushite rule.
date_note: Karima is the valid location at Jebel Barkal; its importance survives the political move toward Meroe.

name: Meroe Royal Temple Precinct
description: Temples, pyramids, and royal installations near the Meroitic capital joined state ritual with dynastic burial and craft production.
date_note: Shendi is the closest valid engine anchor to the Meroe complex.

name: Great Temple of Yeha
description: The enduring monumental precinct of Yeha preserved a prestigious south-Arabian-linked cult landscape in northern Ethiopia.
date_note: The temple is older than AD 1 and is used as inherited sacred geography during the pre-Aksumite to Aksumite transition.

name: Aksum Ancestral Precinct
description: Emerging elite and mortuary landscapes around Aksum gave the developing centre a local ancestral and ceremonial focus.
date_note: Only early phases are represented; the later Christian monuments are excluded.

name: Meccan Sanctuary
description: A protected cult place around the Kaaba represents western Arabian pilgrimage, offerings, and negotiated sanctuary.
date_note: The AD 1 importance is deliberately moderate because detailed descriptions are preserved in later sources.

name: Dedanite Sanctuary
description: Oasis temples and inscriptions at Dedan preserve a locally grounded north-Arabian cult centre on the incense routes.
date_note: Al-Ula is the valid engine anchor; Nabataean and later Islamic layers are not conflated with the AD 1 cult.

name: Petra Sanctuary of Dushara
description: Nabataean temples and high places made Petra a major focus of dynastic, civic, and caravan-linked worship.
date_note: Ma'an is the closest valid engine anchor and does not relocate Petra historically.

name: Awwam Temple of Almaqah
description: The great extra-mural sanctuary of Marib united Sabaean pilgrimage, offerings, legal acts, and the cult of Almaqah.
date_note: The sanctuary was active across the late first millennium BCE and early first millennium CE.

name: Temple of Amm at Timna
description: Qataban's capital precinct made Amm's worship part of royal authority and caravan wealth in the Bayhan valley.
date_note: Bayhan is the valid engine anchor for Timna; later abandonment phases are excluded.

name: Thinissut Sanctuary
description: A rural sanctuary near the Punic-Roman coast preserved local deities, votive practice, and mixed North African cult forms.
date_note: Hammamet is the nearest valid engine anchor; the shared row models continuity rather than a single ethnic cult.

name: Carthaginian Precinct of Tanit and Baal
description: Carthage's Punic cult memory and continuing votive practice remained central to communities rebuilt under Roman rule.
date_note: Tunis is the closest valid engine anchor to Carthage; no late antique Christian layer is included.

name: Carnutes Assembly Grove
description: The central territory of the Carnutes hosted the annual assembly associated with druids, judgment, and inter-community ritual.
date_note: Chartres is a regional engine anchor; Caesar identifies the Carnutes territory but not an excavated grove at the modern city point.

name: Semnonian Sacred Grove
description: A periodically assembled confederate cult in a consecrated grove expressed shared ancestry, restraint, and political prestige.
date_note: Havelberg is a broad regional proxy for Tacitus's Semnones and no later temple institution is implied.

name: Sambian Coastal Grove
description: Groves, waters, amber routes, and ancestral places provide a bounded cult focus for eastern Baltic communities.
date_note: This is a regional archaeological adapter and does not backdate medieval Romuva names or institutions.

name: Saima Sacred Waters
description: Lake passages, islands, hunting grounds, and remembered ancestors form a plausible shared ritual landscape in the Finnish interior.
date_note: The row is deliberately landscape-based because no securely named AD 1 sanctuary is known at the engine point.

name: Kerma Ancestral Precinct
description: Ancient monumental and mortuary ground at Kerma offered Nile communities a deep local focus for ancestry and place.
date_note: The site is inherited sacred geography at AD 1 and does not imply survival of the Bronze Age Kerma state.

name: Jenne-jeno Ancestral Precinct
description: The growing Inland Niger settlement network tied household ancestry, ironworking, exchange, and communal gathering to a durable place.
date_note: The ritual interpretation is intentionally modest and no later imperial or Islamic institution is backdated.

name: Urewe Ancestral Hearths
description: Lakes-region farming and ironworking communities are represented through household ancestors, hearths, and settlement memory.
date_note: Rubaga is a regional engine proxy; Urewe is an archaeological horizon rather than a single people or priesthood.

name: Tsodilo Sacred Hills
description: Rock art, shelters, water, and a striking hill landscape preserve a long ritual relationship between communities and place.
date_note: Hambukushu is the closest valid engine anchor; no single later ethnic ownership is projected onto AD 1.

name: Early Teotihuacan Ceremonial Precinct
description: The rapidly growing Basin of Mexico centre concentrated households, ritual construction, exchange, and emerging civic authority.
date_note: Only first-century BCE and AD 1 formative phases are represented; the mature Avenue and Pyramid of the Sun complex are later.

name: Monte Alban Ceremonial Centre
description: The Zapotec hilltop capital joined plazas, monuments, tombs, and regional assembly above the Oaxaca valleys.
date_note: Zaachila is the nearest valid engine anchor; structures completed after AD 1 are not assumed.

name: Chavin Ceremonial Centre
description: The highland temple complex retained a far-reaching religious memory and pilgrimage landscape near the end of the Chavin horizon.
date_note: Importance reflects enduring prestige around AD 1 and not continued control by a Chavin state.

name: Early Tiwanaku Precinct
description: Lakeshore communities were developing a durable ceremonial centre linking farming, herding, exchange, and collective ritual.
date_note: Only the early settlement and ceremonial phases are represented; the later monumental state is excluded.

name: Scioto Hopewell Earthworks
description: Geometric earthworks, mounds, mortuary rites, and long-distance exchange made the Scioto valley a major gathering landscape.
date_note: Hopewell is used as an archaeological interaction horizon beginning around AD 1 and not as one tribe or state.

name: Oglakhty Ancestral Heights
description: Cemetery landscapes above the Yenisei represent the emerging Tes-Tashtyk transition and community memory in the Minusinsk Basin.
date_note: The campaign date lies near a cultural transition; later Tashtyk traits are not treated as fully formed.

name: Maitum Mortuary Precinct
description: Anthropomorphic burial jars express household ancestry, maritime contact, and distinctive mortuary craft in Sarangani.
date_note: Calibrated dates cross the AD 1 boundary; the row does not impose one archipelago-wide religion.

name: Uluru-Kata Tjuta Living Landscape
description: Rock formations, water places, routes, and inherited law form a deep-time cultural landscape for local custodial communities.
date_note: Lake Amadeus is the nearest valid engine field; the site is local and does not flatten continent-wide traditions into one cult.

name: La Hueca Ancestral Precinct
description: Ceramic and mortuary evidence on Vieques anchors an eastern Caribbean community network at the era boundary.
date_note: The name denotes an archaeological assemblage and does not backdate later Taino or Island Carib identities.

name: Meghalaya Highland Grove
description: Forest clearings, ridges, ancestors, and community rites provide a locally bounded highland sacred landscape.
date_note: The generic geographic name is intentional because named first-century sanctuaries are not securely recoverable.

name: Oxus Temple at Takht-i Sangin
description: The fortified sanctuary on the Oxus combined Iranian and Hellenistic offerings, images, arms, and elite patronage.
date_note: Qubodijon is the closest valid engine anchor; the mixed assemblage is not forced into later orthodox categories.

name: Niya Oasis Ancestral Precinct
description: Irrigated settlement, cemeteries, caravan traffic, and household memory create a defensible local oasis cult focus.
date_note: The row avoids projecting later Buddhist institutions or a securely Iranian identity onto AD 1.

name: Bangga Valley Ancestral Precinct
description: Farming, herding, burials, and long-lived settlement traditions provide a central Tibetan ritual landscape.
date_note: Lhasa is a regional engine proxy; no later Tibetan imperial or monastic institution is backdated.

name: Yushu Mortuary Landscape
description: Highland pastoral communities marked ancestry and territory through cemeteries, seasonal routes, and material exchange.
date_note: This is a broad eastern plateau archaeological anchor rather than a named first-century temple.

name: Vidarbha Megalithic Precinct
description: Megalithic burials, iron objects, livestock, and settlement ties made mortuary grounds durable community landmarks.
date_note: Chandrapur is a regional engine anchor and no later dynastic temple is implied.

name: Plain of Jars Mortuary Landscape
description: Monumental stone jars and associated burial practices created a distinctive upland gathering and mortuary landscape.
date_note: Phonsavan is the valid engine anchor; dates span the Iron Age and the row avoids assigning a later ethnicity.

name: Middle Amur Ancestral Precinct
description: Settlements, cemeteries, fishing, hunting, and iron-working horizons anchor a local riverine ritual landscape.
date_note: Aigun is a regional proxy and the row does not impose a uniform Tungusic identity.

name: Niah Mortuary Caves
description: Caves, burials, objects, and rainforest-coast exchange sustained a long-lived sacred and mortuary landscape in northwest Borneo.
date_note: The row represents varied local Metal Age communities rather than a single Bornean religion.

name: Bomberai Ancestor Caves
description: Cave occupation, pottery, shell, ochre, and coastal movement provide a durable place-based focus for local ancestors.
date_note: The archaeology supports a regional adapter only and not one trans-New-Guinea identity.

name: Guahan Ancestral Shore
description: Deeply established island communities tied ancestry, settlement, reef use, and voyaging knowledge to Guahan's coasts.
date_note: No later latte-stone political system is projected wholesale onto AD 1.

name: Yap Ancestral Precinct
description: Early island settlement and seafaring connections are represented through household ancestors and a locally rooted ceremonial place.
date_note: The chronology remains cautious and later stone-money networks are not backdated.

name: Acutuba Ancestral Precinct
description: Ceramic communities around the central Amazon linked river routes, settlements, cultivated landscapes, and ancestral memory.
date_note: Manaos is the regional engine anchor; Acutuba is an archaeological phase rather than a named polity or ethnicity.
